questions.prompt: From 14 test cylinders, the 95 % confidence interval for the mean compressive strength of a concrete mix is 31.2 to 34.6 MPa. Which statement is correct?
options: We are 95 % confident that the mean strength of the mix is between 31.2 and 34.6 MPa
There is a 95 % probability that the mean strength is between 31.2 and 34.6 MPa
95 % of the cylinders made from this mix are between 31.2 and 34.6 MPa
95 % of samples of 14 cylinders will have a mean between 31.2 and 34.6 MPa
questions.explanation: The confidence belongs to the method: about 95 % of intervals built this way contain μ. Once calculated, this interval either contains μ or not, so a probability statement about μ is not right. The interval is about the mean, not single cylinders, and it is centered on this sample's x̄, not on μ, so it does not predict other samples' means.

questions.prompt: A 90 % confidence interval for the proportion of defective connectors in a lot is 0.021 to 0.047. Which statements are right? Choose every one that applies.
options: We are 90 % confident that between 2.1 % and 4.7 % of the lot's connectors are defective
If the sampling were repeated many times, about 90 % of the intervals made this way would contain the lot's true proportion
The lot's true proportion of defectives is 0.034, the middle of the interval
There is a 10 % chance that this particular interval is wrong because of an arithmetic slip
questions.explanation: The first is the in-context statement, the second what the 90 % means. The middle of the interval is p̂, an estimate, not the true proportion. The 10 % is the share of intervals that miss p because of the luck of the sample; it has nothing to do with arithmetic.

questions.prompt: From the same sample, an engineer calculates a 95 % and a 99 % confidence interval for a mean. How do they compare?
options: The 99 % interval is wider: more confidence needs a larger critical value
The 99 % interval is narrower: more confidence means a more precise estimate
They are the same width, because they come from the same sample
The 99 % interval is centered higher, because it covers more of the values
questions.explanation: Both are centered on the same x̄. The 99 % interval uses a larger critical value (2.576 against 1.960 for z), so it is wider. Being surer that the interval contains μ costs precision.

questions.prompt: Forty independent teams each take their own random sample from the same process and build a **90 %** confidence interval for its mean. About how many of the forty intervals would you expect to contain the true mean? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: Each interval contains μ with probability 0.90 before its sample is taken, so about 0.90 × 40 = 36 will contain it and about 4 will miss. No team can tell from its own interval whether it is one of the four.

questions.prompt:
The Simulation drew samples from a population whose mean μ it knows, and built a 90 % interval from each. The figure shows the first 100; the vertical line is μ, and the red intervals miss it. What do the red intervals show?
[[figure: st.m7.interpreting.ninety 2]]
options: Samples that by chance fell far from μ; correct calculations from unlucky samples
Intervals calculated with a mistake, such as z used in place of t
Samples taken from a different population, with a different mean
Intervals that should be thrown away before the others are reported
questions.explanation: Every interval was built by the same correct method from a sample of the same population. A 90 % method misses μ about 10 % of the time just from the luck of the sample. In real work you cannot tell which kind of interval you have, which is why the confidence describes the method.

questions.prompt: A pump manufacturer claims its seals last 250 hours on average under a test load. A lab tests a sample of seals, and the 95 % confidence interval for the mean life is 231 to 246 hours. What should the lab conclude?
options: The data argue against the claim: 250 h is above every plausible value of the mean at 95 % confidence
The claim is supported, because 250 h is close to the interval's upper end of 246 h
Nothing, because a confidence interval cannot be compared with a claimed value
The claim is proved false: the true mean is certainly below 246 h
questions.explanation: Values outside a 95 % interval are not plausible at that confidence, and 250 h is above the whole interval. That is strong evidence against the claim, not proof: a 95 % method misses about 1 time in 20.

questions.prompt: A traffic engineer's 95 % confidence interval for the mean morning travel time on a corridor is 18.4 to 21.0 minutes. Which sentence is the best one for the city's report?
options: "The mean morning travel time on the corridor is between about 18.4 and 21.0 minutes (95 % confidence), so the 20-minute target may or may not be met; more data are needed to tell."
"The 95 % confidence interval is (18.4, 21.0)."
"There is a 95 % probability that the corridor's mean travel time is under 21.0 minutes, so the 20-minute target is met."
"95 % of the morning trips on the corridor take between 18.4 and 21.0 minutes, so the 20-minute target is met."
questions.explanation: The first names the quantity, the units and the confidence, and reads the result against the target: 20 minutes is inside the interval, so the data cannot say on which side the mean is. The second is right but says nothing in context. The third makes a probability statement about μ, and the fourth reads the interval as a range for single trips.
